was headed the opposite direction from our route which is another way of expressing
the aviators favorite complaint - 1.e., we have a head wind. However, when you are
bueking a head wind you usually fly low and that is how it happened that I saw the
wheel barrow with full rigged square sail, The wolfe who was acting as helmsman
of this "Kansas Yacht" was stepping along at a lively rate while four people sat on
the barrow - two on each side of the "keel". The sail was about five feet high by
tour feet wide. I have seen pictures of these contraptions but this is the first
one I have ever seen in actual use. The "captain" did not have to worry like the
old Cape Cod captain who said he would not sail a brig because he was a good
Christian and the bible directed that no good Christian "could serve two masters."
I had a fine rest at leiping. When I arrived found Irances, Bo and Ruth
were away on a trip to Tai Yuan lu, Capital of Shansi Province. Shansi means
"west of the mountaina" while Shantung means "east of the mountains". In that section
there had been heavy rains with reports in Peiping that the rivers were overflowing
their banks, many cities wiped out, bandits on the loose and the usual number of
rumors which thrive and gain momentun in a country where transportation and
comunication is so uncertain. Debby was quite worried but Sunday we received a
very welcome if inelegant telegram "hold your noses here te come". And sure
enough Sunday evening about 7:30 the girls descended on us with eighteen bundles
of 100t gathered in Shansi, the packages ranging in size from small boxes to good
sized Shansi chests. If we had locked the bathroom doors, I think the girls would
have traded all their plunder for the keys.
After one day in Peiping, they started
off early Tuesday morning for a trip to the Diamond Mountains of Korea, It will be
another interesting experience for them, and I'm wondering what the high light will
be. On the lasttrip it was gun fire. The girls were crossing a big plain in Shansi
when they heard a loud whizzing noise over head, often repeated. In the distance
they could hear rifly fire. Tinally it dawned on them that the whizzing sound
was caused by bullets and they proe eded in true negro fashion to say "feet carry
me away". It turned out that they were crossing a rifle range and probably stood
a much better chance of getting hit than if they had been the targets.
We aze all very sad over the thought of Ruth going home early in
September. She has been a real addition to our party in China and we*ll miss her.
I imagine there will be times during hez debutant winter when some boring dimer
par ther will catch & far away 100k in her eye and never quite know what the score is,
but I know too that she will carry on in St. Louis as she has here taling things
good, bad and indirterent, maling the most of them all.
Nearing Shanghai now so md11 wind up this letter - as ever
Narold

Flying to Feiping
August 8th, 1935.
Dear Family:
I have been pretty much on the go ever since early Spring and as a
result my weary readers, have had a much needed rest which the author just now
I am going to spend a few days with
the family just to get back on speaking terms and say to the ehildren "my how
you've grown!"
There is really not much to write about other than Chinese and Philippine
polities. You wouldn't be interested and I am not qualified to diseuss either
brand beyond saying that they compare very favorably with our own. In the
Philippines as in Missouri there are a certain number of patriots who are
vociferously willing to dedicate their lives to the public welfare, get their
names on a pay roll and their feet on a desk. After the Philippine Commonwealth
Is established the number of patriots will undoubtedly increase.
I had six weeks in Manila during which time we accomplished a great
deal but did not secure favorable action on the franchise which we tried to
secure from the Philippine Legislature.
However, there seans to be no real
opposition and we hope that the next session which is called for September 23r
wi11 approve our bill.
This is Thursday. Got back to Shanghai Monday afternoon.
there was plenty to do and I brought a lot of correspondence with me to read on
the plane and try to answer or dispose of in one way or another.
Last night one of our best Chinese friends M.Y. Tang came by to see me
and learning that I was in a meeting wrote me a note.
It seems that his niece,
either actual or adopted, is going to attend some Catholic College in Webster
this Winter. Her name is Eppy Chang. She is related to Mrs. I.V. Soong and comes
from one of the best families in China. Debby and I had Luneh with her almost a
year ago at a party which Me. MY. Zang gave for Hebe and Catherine. She is a
very charming girl, speaks English well and is very good looking. I have written
Letters of introduction for her to Ruth, Lucy, Mary Scott, Mrs. Beauregard
(Lindbergh Trophies) and to Archbishop Glennon. I hope very much that the
members of the St. Louis Bixby clan will show Miss Chang a good time - maybe have
her around for Sunday dinner or invite her to the Country Club some Saturday night.
If she dances as well as most Chinese girls you will fine your boy friends forming
Flying back to Shanghai Friday August 16th. I was booked to
return on Wednesday but at the request of one of our ofticials gave up my reserva-
tion in favor of an important passenger vho had to be in Shanghai on Wednesday.
The Douglas transport flies up to Peiping on Tuesday, back on Wednesday and up
again on Saturday returning Sunday. The other trip is made via Stinson up on
Thursday and back on Friday so, of course, I struck the small Stinson both ways.
Its funny how soon and how easily you become spoiled. The Stinson nine hour
schedule used to seem de lux indeed as compared with 44 hours by train. Now,
however, the Douglas 14 passenger liner with comfortable seats, no noise, 5 hour
schedule and steward serving tea, coffee, beer, sandwiches etc. makes the Stinson
